cards.front: When a diuretic blocks one nephron segment's apical sodium entry, in which two places does the kidney feel it?
cards.back: Downstream: more sodium and fluid reach ENaC, so more potassium is secreted. Locally: if that segment built a transepithelial voltage, the ions that voltage moved now move much less.
cards.quote: Block a door and the kidney feels it in two places.

cards.front: The electrical potential difference between tubular fluid and surrounding tissue is the {{c1::transepithelial voltage}}.
cards.quote: That electrical potential difference between tubular fluid and surrounding tissue is the transepithelial voltage.

cards.front: Which basolateral protein maintains the inward sodium gradient that every apical sodium entry protein along the nephron spends?
cards.back: The Na+-K+-ATPase (sodium-potassium pump), which exports sodium across the basolateral membrane in every segment.
cards.quote: In every segment the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase exports sodium and maintains the inward sodium gradient that every apical door spends.
cards.section: One pump, five doors

cards.front: Name the two apical sodium entry proteins of the proximal tubule and what each brings in.
cards.back: NHE3 (sodium-hydrogen exchanger 3): luminal Na+ in exchange for intracellular H+. SGLT2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2): Na+ with glucose.
cards.quote: NHE3 (sodium-hydrogen exchanger 3) and SGLT2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2)
cards.section: One pump, five doors

cards.front: In one cycle of NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, {{c1::one Na+, one K+ and two Cl-}} enter together.
cards.back: Electrically neutral entry.
cards.quote: In one cycle of NKCC2, one Na+, one K+ and two Cl- enter together.
cards.section: Building the voltage, one ion at a time

cards.front: Roughly what share of filtered sodium does each human nephron segment reabsorb: proximal tubule, thick ascending limb, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct?
cards.back: About 65%, 25%, 5% and 3% (rounded from review ranges of 60–70%, 20–25%, 5–7% and 2–5%).
cards.quote: The shares are rounded from human review estimates of roughly 60–70% proximal, 20–25% thick limb, about 5–7% distal convoluted tubule and 2–5% collecting duct.
cards.section: One pump, five doors

cards.front: Why does NCC in the distal convoluted tubule build no transepithelial voltage, whereas ENaC in collecting-duct principal cells makes the lumen negative?
cards.back: NCC carries Na+ with Cl-, so it moves no net charge. ENaC lets Na+ in alone, moving positive charge out of the lumen without a partner.
cards.quote: none from NCC, which moves no net charge
cards.section: One pump, five doors

cards.front: Why does more sodium reaching ENaC in the late distal nephron and collecting duct increase potassium secretion?
cards.back: ENaC admits sodium without a partner ion, so the lumen goes negative. That negativity drives potassium out of the cell into the urine through ROMK.
cards.why: Aldosterone, raised by sustained salt loss, adds to the effect.
cards.quote: ENaC lets sodium in without a partner ion, so the lumen goes negative, and that drives potassium out of the cell into the urine through ROMK, a potassium channel.
cards.section: Blocking a door: look downstream, then locally

cards.front: A loop diuretic acts in the thick limb and a thiazide acts in the distal convoluted tubule. Why do both tend to cause potassium loss?
cards.back: Both send extra sodium downstream to ENaC, which makes the lumen more negative and increases potassium secretion through ROMK.
cards.quote: The loop diuretic and the thiazide both send extra sodium to ENaC, so both tend toward potassium loss.
cards.section: Blocking a door: look downstream, then locally

cards.front: Using rounded human sodium shares, why can a loop diuretic cause a larger natriuresis than a thiazide?
cards.back: Blocking the thick limb releases up to about a quarter of filtered sodium toward segments that normally reabsorb only about 8% (5% + 3%). Blocking NCC releases only about 5%.
cards.quote: Block the thick limb and up to about a quarter of filtered sodium heads on, toward segments that normally take back only about 8% between them (5% + 3%).
cards.section: Blocking a door: look downstream, then locally

cards.front: Proximal reabsorption is nearly {{c1::isosmotic}}: fluid is removed with approximately unchanged total solute concentration.
cards.quote: Proximal reabsorption is nearly isosmotic reabsorption, meaning removal of fluid with approximately unchanged total solute concentration.
cards.section: Proximal tubule: the bulk door and the glucose door

cards.front: In mice lacking NHE3, in situ microperfusion found proximal bicarbonate and fluid absorption reduced by 54% and 63%. What does this show about bulk proximal uptake?
cards.back: NHE3 loss cut proximal bicarbonate and fluid absorption by about half or more, so glucose cotransport cannot account for bulk proximal uptake alone.
cards.quote: In mice lacking NHE3, in situ microperfusion found proximal bicarbonate and fluid absorption reduced by 54% and 63%, evidence that glucose cotransport cannot account for bulk proximal uptake alone.
cards.section: Proximal tubule: the bulk door and the glucose door

cards.front: Why does SGLT2 matter far more for renal glucose handling than for sodium balance?
cards.back: It carries only about 5% of total renal NaCl reabsorption in non-diabetic conditions, but it supplies early proximal glucose uptake.
cards.quote: It carries only about 5% of total renal NaCl reabsorption in non-diabetic conditions, so it matters far more for glucose than for sodium.
cards.section: Proximal tubule: the bulk door and the glucose door

cards.front: {{c1::Transport maximum (Tm)}} is the maximal reabsorption rate for a substance under specified conditions.
cards.quote: Transport maximum (Tm) is the maximal reabsorption rate for a substance under specified conditions.
cards.section: Glucose: a carrier with a ceiling

cards.front: The renal glucose {{c1::threshold}} is the plasma glucose concentration where glucose first appears in urine.
cards.quote: Threshold is the plasma glucose concentration where glucose first appears in urine.
cards.section: Glucose: a carrier with a ceiling

cards.front: In a sharp-saturation (no-splay) glucose model, threshold = {{c1::Tm / GFR}}.
cards.back: At threshold, filtered load equals Tm.
cards.quote: No-splay threshold = Tm / GFR = 350 mg/min / 125 mL/min = 2.8 mg/mL = 280 mg/dL
cards.section: Glucose: a carrier with a ceiling

cards.front: Illustrative adult kidney, no splay: GFR 125 mL/min, glucose Tm 350 mg/min, plasma glucose 300 mg/dL, glucose freely filtered and not secreted. What are filtered load, reabsorption and excretion?
cards.back: 300 mg/dL = 3.0 mg/mL. Filtered load = 125 x 3.0 = 375 mg/min. Reabsorption is capped at 350 mg/min, so excretion = 375 − 350 = 25 mg/min.
cards.quote: Reabsorption is capped at 350 mg/min, leaving 150 mg/min for excretion.
cards.section: Glucose: a carrier with a ceiling

cards.front: In a no-splay glucose model, GFR is 120 mL/min and Tm is 360 mg/min. What is the threshold in mg/dL?
cards.back: Threshold = Tm / GFR = 360 / 120 = 3.0 mg/mL = 300 mg/dL.
cards.quote: At the model's threshold, filtered load equals Tm
cards.section: Glucose: a carrier with a ceiling

cards.front: In a no-splay glucose model with Tm 350 mg/min, GFR falls from 125 to 60 mL/min while Tm stays fixed. Does the threshold rise or fall, and is glucose excreted at plasma 400 mg/dL?
cards.back: Threshold rises, to 350 / 60 = 5.83 mg/mL, about 580 mg/dL. At 400 mg/dL filtered load is only 240 mg/min, below Tm, so no glucose is excreted.
cards.quote: Lower filtration raises the threshold when capacity stays fixed.
cards.section: Glucose: a carrier with a ceiling

cards.front: In the no-splay model (GFR 125 mL/min, Tm 350 mg/min), kidney disease destroys half of all nephrons. Predict the new glucose threshold.
cards.back: Unchanged at about 280 mg/dL. Losing whole nephrons lowers GFR and Tm together (62.5 mL/min and 175 mg/min), and Tm / GFR stays 2.8 mg/mL.
cards.why: Rests on threshold = Tm / GFR; only a fall in GFR with fixed capacity raises it.
cards.quote: Do not carry that into kidney disease: losing whole nephrons lowers Tm too.
cards.section: Glucose: a carrier with a ceiling

cards.front: Healthy adult human kidneys spill low levels of glucose around 180–200 mg/dL, below the illustrative Tm/GFR threshold of 280 mg/dL. Why?
cards.back: Splay: nephrons differ in capacity relative to their filtered loads, and finite carrier affinity rounds uptake near saturation. Tm/GFR is an idealized upper estimate.
cards.quote: Individual nephrons differ in capacity relative to their filtered loads, and finite carrier affinity rounds uptake near saturation.
cards.section: Glucose: a carrier with a ceiling

cards.front: Micropuncture in anesthetized mice: early proximal collections showed 78% of filtered glucose reabsorbed in wild type and none in Sglt2 knockouts. What does this establish?
cards.back: SGLT2 is necessary for early proximal glucose uptake in mice.
cards.why: Knockouts had unchanged plasma glucose and GFR, arguing against increased filtration as the cause of their glucose loss.
cards.quote: Early collections showed 78% of filtered glucose already reabsorbed in wild type versus none in knockouts.
cards.section: The evidence: delete the gene, sample the tubule

cards.front: In 12 healthy adults, a week of an SGLT2 inhibitor lowered glucose Tm by about 55%, but the estimated threshold fell much further. What explained glucose in urine at ordinary plasma levels?
cards.back: The lowered threshold, not the lower Tm or the changed splay.
cards.quote: The authors concluded that the lowered threshold, not the lower Tm or the changed splay, explained the glucose that appeared in urine at ordinary plasma levels.
cards.section: The evidence: delete the gene, sample the tubule

cards.front: Use the downstream-sodium rule: what potassium effect should an SGLT2 inhibitor have, compared with a loop diuretic?
cards.back: Small. It sends much glucose to the urine but little sodium downstream to ENaC, so little extra potassium secretion is predicted (not measured in the studies cited).
cards.quote: An SGLT2 inhibitor sends much glucose to the urine but little sodium, so the downstream half of the rule predicts a small potassium effect
cards.section: SGLT2 inhibitors and the rule

cards.front: Isolated rabbit medullary thick ascending limbs at slow perfusion lowered outgoing sodium and chloride to about 0.79 and 0.77 of incoming, with no osmotic water flow even under imposed gradients. What does this make the segment?
cards.back: The kidney's diluting segment: it removes salt but not water, so tubular fluid becomes more dilute.
cards.quote: Even under imposed osmotic gradients, no osmotic water flow occurred, so the fluid grew more dilute: this is the kidney's diluting segment.
cards.section: Thick ascending limb: a salt pump that charges the lumen

cards.front: NKCC2 is electrically neutral. How does the thick ascending limb still make its lumen positive?
cards.back: Chloride exits basolaterally (via channels including ClC-Kb), moving negative charge to the blood, while potassium recycles back into the lumen through apical ROMK, returning positive charge to the lumen.
cards.why: Recycling is needed because tubular fluid holds little potassium compared with sodium and chloride.
cards.quote: Negative charge goes to the blood and positive charge back to the lumen, so the lumen ends up a few millivolts positive.
cards.section: Building the voltage, one ion at a time

cards.front: In isolated rabbit thick ascending limbs, removing luminal potassium reduced transport current, and adding barium to block potassium recycling almost abolished it. What do these results show?
cards.back: Thick-limb salt uptake depends on potassium on the luminal side, supplied by NKCC2's need for K+ and kept available by apical potassium recycling.
cards.quote: In isolated rabbit tubules, removing luminal potassium reduced the transport current, and also blocking potassium recycling with barium almost abolished it
cards.section: Building the voltage, one ion at a time

cards.front: Why does the thick limb's lumen-positive voltage matter especially for calcium and magnesium reabsorption?
cards.back: Cation-selective junctions let the positive lumen push cations between cells toward the blood, and divalent ions feel twice the push of sodium.
cards.quote: Calcium and magnesium carry two charges each, so the same voltage pushes on them twice as hard as on sodium.
cards.section: What the voltage moves: calcium and magnesium

cards.front: At body temperature RT/F is about 26.7 mV and, for a passive ion at equilibrium, lumen/blood = exp(−zV / 26.7 mV). If the thick-limb lumen were +10 mV, what lumen/blood ratio could voltage alone hold for ionized calcium?
cards.back: z = 2, V = +10 mV: exp(−20 / 26.7) = exp(−0.749) ≈ 0.47. An equilibrium limit, not a measured luminal value.
cards.quote: For a passive ion at equilibrium, lumen/blood = exp(−zV / 26.7 mV), where z is its charge and V the lumen voltage.
cards.section: What the voltage moves: calcium and magnesium

cards.front: About what share of filtered magnesium and of filtered calcium does the thick ascending limb reabsorb (textbook estimates)?
cards.back: About 60–70% of filtered magnesium and about 20–25% of filtered calcium.
cards.quote: Textbook estimates credit it with about 60–70% of filtered magnesium and about 20–25% of filtered calcium.
cards.section: What the voltage moves: calcium and magnesium

cards.front: Furosemide blocks NKCC2 from the lumen in an intact mammalian kidney. Predict the lumen voltage and urinary sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium.
cards.back: The lumen-positive voltage largely collapses. All four rise in the urine: sodium most of any class here; calcium and magnesium lose their paracellular drive; potassium rises because extra sodium reaches ENaC.
cards.quote: So in an intact mammalian kidney all four rise in the urine, subject to downstream compensation.
cards.section: What the voltage moves: calcium and magnesium

cards.front: Inherited loss of apical ROMK (a form of Bartter syndrome) leaves NKCC2 intact. Using the thick-limb circuit, why does it resemble a loop diuretic in urinary sodium and calcium?
cards.back: Without ROMK, potassium cannot recycle to the lumen, so NKCC2 runs short of potassium and the lumen-positive voltage fails. Result: salt wasting and high urinary calcium.
cards.why: Rests on potassium recycling powering both NKCC2 entry and the positive voltage; plasma potassium is usually low, though ROMK loss can raise it at first in newborns.
cards.quote: Inherited loss of NKCC2 or ROMK (two forms of Bartter syndrome) causes a similar pattern without a drug: salt wasting and high urinary calcium, usually with low plasma potassium
cards.section: What the voltage moves: calcium and magnesium

cards.front: A thiazide blocks NCC, which moves one Na+ and one Cl- together. What does the voltage rule predict for urinary calcium, and what actually happens?
cards.back: The rule predicts no change, since no lumen-positive voltage is lost. In fact urinary calcium falls, as Gitelman syndrome shows.
cards.quote: The real answer is lower urinary calcium, as Gitelman syndrome shows.
cards.section: Distal convoluted tubule: the door with no voltage

cards.front: What are the two candidate explanations for lower urinary calcium during sustained thiazide use?
cards.back: Proximal: salt loss shrinks body fluid volume, so the proximal tubule reabsorbs more sodium and calcium. Distal: less chloride entry is proposed to make the cell interior more negative, which would favor calcium entry. Still unsettled.
cards.quote: Salt loss shrinks body fluid volume. The proximal tubule then reabsorbs more sodium and, with it, more calcium.
cards.section: Distal convoluted tubule: the door with no voltage

cards.front: What syndrome results from loss-of-function variants in the human NCC gene, and what is its plasma potassium, plasma magnesium and urinary calcium pattern?
cards.back: Gitelman syndrome: low plasma potassium, low plasma magnesium, low urinary calcium.
cards.quote: Loss-of-function variants in the human NCC gene cause Gitelman syndrome, with low plasma potassium and magnesium and low urinary calcium
cards.section: Distal convoluted tubule: the door with no voltage

cards.front: Sustained NCC block increases urinary magnesium even though the distal convoluted tubule loses no voltage. What is the lesson's account?
cards.back: A greater fraction of filtered magnesium escapes reabsorption through distal transport adaptation, not through loss of magnesium passage via NCC itself.
cards.quote: With sustained NCC block, a greater fraction of filtered magnesium escapes reabsorption, although no voltage is lost.
cards.section: Distal convoluted tubule: the door with no voltage

cards.front: Reported variants in the WNK kinase pathway increase NCC activity. Running the downstream rule in reverse, predict the effect on plasma potassium and arterial pressure.
cards.back: Less sodium reaches ENaC, which can reduce potassium secretion (potassium retention), and greater salt retention can favor higher arterial pressure.
cards.why: The downstream half of the rule, applied to increased rather than blocked entry.
cards.quote: can reduce downstream sodium delivery and favor potassium retention and higher arterial pressure
cards.section: Distal convoluted tubule: the door with no voltage

cards.front: Rat early and late surface distal segments were microperfused separately. A thiazide-type NCC blocker cut early sodium and chloride transport to zero but had no significant effect late; chloride removal reduced sodium transport only early. What does this establish, and what not?
cards.back: Early and late segments use different apical entry mechanisms: a chloride-dependent, thiazide-sensitive function sits early. It does not identify the protein or test deep nephrons or other species.
cards.quote: Instead, the blocker reduced sodium and chloride transport to zero early, with no significant effect late; removing chloride reduced sodium transport early but not late.
cards.section: The evidence: find the function, then the gene

cards.front: Why should a lifelong NCC knockout and an acute NCC blocker not be assumed equivalent for ENaC uptake and potassium excretion in rodents?
cards.back: Chronic deletion permits compensation, so its steady state differs from acute block; one rodent report found no rise in ENaC uptake or potassium excretion after acute NCC block.
cards.why: The same limit applies to the Sglt2 knockout: lifelong deletion permits compensation.
cards.quote: a rodent report summarized in a review found neither increased ENaC-mediated uptake nor increased potassium excretion after acute NCC block
cards.section: Acute NCC block

cards.front: Amiloride blocks ENaC from the lumen of a collecting duct with sodium and potassium delivery held fixed. Predict lumen voltage, sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion.
cards.back: Lumen becomes less negative; sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion both fall, so amiloride spares potassium.
cards.quote: Under fixed delivery, ENaC block reduces sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion, so amiloride spares potassium.
cards.section: Collecting duct: the channel that makes the lumen negative

cards.front: Liddle syndrome involves gain-of-function variants in the ENaC beta or gamma subunit. Using the ENaC rules, predict lumen voltage, sodium handling and potassium secretion.
cards.back: Excess sodium entry makes the lumen more negative, increases sodium reabsorption (favoring high blood pressure) and drives more potassium secretion through ROMK.
cards.why: The mirror image of amiloride block, based on ENaC's lumen-negative voltage.
cards.quote: Reported human gain-of-function variants in the ENaC beta or gamma subunit (Liddle syndrome, an inherited form of high blood pressure) provide a complementary test of excessive sodium entry.
cards.section: Collecting duct: the channel that makes the lumen negative

cards.front: Furosemide raises urinary calcium, while hydrochlorothiazide lowers it. Explain the difference in terms of each segment's transport.
cards.back: Furosemide collapses the thick limb's lumen-positive voltage that drove paracellular calcium reabsorption. NCC builds no voltage, so thiazide hypocalciuria comes from a volume-linked proximal effect, a distal effect, or both.
cards.quote: furosemide collapses a voltage that moved calcium; hydrochlorothiazide blocks a door that built none
cards.section: The table, filled

cards.front: A loop diuretic can send more sodium downstream per dose than a thiazide. Why do thiazides cause low plasma potassium at least as often at usual doses?
cards.back: Thiazides act longer, so their downstream sodium delivery to ENaC is sustained.
cards.quote: The loop diuretic can send more sodium downstream per dose, but thiazides act longer, so at usual doses they cause low plasma potassium at least as often.
cards.section: The table, filled

cards.front: Using isolated rabbit thick ascending limbs with separately controlled lumen and bath, how would you test whether an NKCC2-blocking loop diuretic acts from the lumen or the bath?
cards.back: Apply the blocker to lumen and bath at matched concentrations in separate runs, with baseline and washout, reversing run order across tubules. Expect luminal application to suppress salt uptake and positive voltage.
cards.why: Washout recovery distinguishes reversible inhibition from damage; conclusions hold for rabbit segments in vitro.
cards.quote: Compare luminal and bath application of the NKCC2 blocker at matched concentrations in separate runs with washout, reversing run order across tubules.
cards.section: Design problem
